title: US Justice Department forms task force to pursue misuse of advanced AI
excerpt: The US Department of Justice announced a task force on 5 November 2026 to coordinate criminal and civil cases involving the misuse of advanced AI. Many practical details are still unknown.

sources.title: Nextgov/FCW: Department of Justice forms AI task force
Decrypt: DOJ Creates 'Super Intelligence' Task Force to Guard Against AI Abuse

body_html:
The United States Department of Justice (DOJ), the federal government's law enforcement department, announced a new task force on Thursday 5 November 2026 to deal with people and organisations that misuse advanced AI. It is called the Super Intelligence Task Force. The name follows a September 2026 executive order from President Donald Trump that directs federal agencies to refer to AI as "super intelligence" (SI), according to Nextgov/FCW.

What the task force will do

According to Nextgov/FCW and Decrypt, which both report on the department's announcement, the task force will:

  • coordinate criminal and civil enforcement cases that involve AI;
  • recommend enforcement priorities to prevent misuse of AI;
  • write guidance for prosecutors on unlawful conduct involving AI;
  • take over the work of the department's AI Litigation Task Force, set up in January 2026, and coordinate the department's civil lawsuits related to AI;
  • act as the department's main contact with the federal Super Intelligence Force chaired by Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence.

The targets named are foreign governments and their proxies, transnational criminal groups, and individuals or companies that use AI for fraud or other unlawful acts. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the aim is to ensure "America's leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI". He also said the task force will take steps, where appropriate, to promote American leadership in the technology. The task force is co-chaired by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss.

Decrypt reports that Mr Weiss said the department has a responsibility to "harden regular reporting on SI risk and response", and that the task force wants AI companies to strengthen internal controls so their systems behave as intended.

What is not yet known

The reports do not give the task force's budget, staff numbers or timeline. Decrypt notes the announcement does not explain how it will work with other agencies. It is also not yet clear what "regular reporting on SI risk" would involve, who would report, or whether any new duties for AI companies are planned. Humasure could not open the department's own press release for this story, so the details above rest on the two reports.

Why it matters for staying in charge

Most AI safety rules focus on how products are designed and tested before they reach people. A law enforcement task force works at the other end: it deals with people who misuse AI once harm or a crime has happened. Both matter. Clear accountability for misuse supports Humasure Directive D9 Accountable, which says someone must answer for what an AI product does. The focus on attacks against critical infrastructure links to D6 Secure and supported: an AI system that can be hijacked is one nobody is in charge of.

Prosecutions do not replace independent testing of products before they are sold. For questions you can ask about any AI product's security and who is responsible for it, see our Security and Questions to ask pages.
